about: Questions a home child care provider asks about the CACFP meal pattern, with the answer USDA gives. Every ground-truth answer is taken from the regulation text (7 CFR 226.20 as of 2026-10-22) or from USDA policy memorandum CACFP 06-2025 (December 20, 2024), cited per case. Nothing here was written by Tally's authors as an answer; we wrote the question in a provider's words and copied USDA's answer. Each case carries the correct answer and a wrong answer with the opposite polarity, so the same set measures both wrong answers served and correct answers wrongly blocked. The off-topic cases are questions the regulation does not decide, where the only right verdict is 'cannot be proved'.

cases.question: Can I serve the strawberry yogurt cups as the meat alternate at snack? The label says 17 grams of added sugars per 6 ounces.
cases.facts: The meal is a snack. The children are 3 to 5 years old. The yogurt has 17 grams of added sugars per 6 ounces.
cases.correct: No. Yogurt is creditable as a meat alternate only if it has no more than 12 grams of added sugars per 6 ounces, and 17 grams is over the limit.
cases.wrong: Yes. Yogurt credits as a meat alternate and 17 grams is under the 23 gram limit.

cases.question: Can I serve the plain yogurt as the meat alternate at snack? The label says 9 grams of added sugars per 6 ounces.
cases.facts: The meal is a snack. The children are 3 to 5 years old. The yogurt has 9 grams of added sugars per 6 ounces.
cases.correct: Yes. Yogurt is creditable as a meat alternate because 9 grams of added sugars per 6 ounces is within the 12 gram limit.
cases.wrong: No. Yogurt is not creditable as a meat alternate because 9 grams of added sugars per 6 ounces is over the limit.

cases.question: What is the sugar limit for yogurt now?
cases.correct: Yogurt must contain no more than 12 grams of added sugars per 6 ounces to be creditable.
cases.wrong: Yogurt must contain no more than 23 grams of total sugars per 6 ounces to be creditable.
cases.source: 7 CFR 226.20(a)(5)(iii)(B); the 23 g total sugars limit expired September 30, 2025

cases.question: The kids love frozen yogurt. Can it count as the meat alternate at snack?
cases.facts: The meal is a snack. The food is frozen yogurt.
cases.correct: No. Frozen yogurt is not creditable as yogurt, so it does not count as a meat alternate.
cases.wrong: Yes. Frozen yogurt is creditable as a meat alternate like any other yogurt.

cases.question: Is the frosted cereal okay for breakfast? The box says 8 grams of added sugars per ounce.
cases.facts: The meal is breakfast. The breakfast cereal has 8 grams of added sugars per dry ounce.
cases.correct: No. A breakfast cereal is creditable as a grain only if it has no more than 6 grams of added sugars per dry ounce, and 8 grams is over the limit.
cases.wrong: Yes. The cereal is creditable as a grain because 8 grams of added sugars per dry ounce is under the limit.

cases.question: Is the oat cereal okay for breakfast? The box says 4 grams of added sugars per ounce and it is made with whole grain oats.
cases.facts: The meal is breakfast. The breakfast cereal has 4 grams of added sugars per dry ounce and is made with whole grain meal.
cases.correct: Yes. The breakfast cereal is creditable as a grain because 4 grams of added sugars per dry ounce is within the 6 gram limit and it is made with whole grain.
cases.wrong: No. The breakfast cereal is not creditable as a grain because 4 grams of added sugars per dry ounce is over the limit.

cases.question: Is the cereal limit still 6 grams of total sugar?
cases.correct: The breakfast cereal limit is 6 grams of added sugars per dry ounce, not total sugars.
cases.wrong: Yes, breakfast cereals must have no more than 6 grams of total sugars per dry ounce.
cases.source: 7 CFR 226.20(a)(4)(ii); the total sugars limit expired September 30, 2025

cases.question: Is milk and apple juice okay for afternoon snack?
cases.facts: The meal is a snack. The children are 3 to 5 years old. The snack contains fluid milk and fruit juice and nothing else.
cases.correct: No. A snack whose only two items are fluid milk and juice is not reimbursable.
cases.wrong: Yes, the snack is reimbursable because milk and juice are two components.

cases.question: Whole grain crackers and cheese for snack, is that enough?
cases.facts: The meal is a snack. The children are 3 to 5 years old. The snack contains grains and a meat alternate, two components, and is not only milk and juice.
cases.correct: Yes. A snack with two of the five components is reimbursable, and grains plus a meat alternate is two components.
cases.wrong: No. A snack needs milk to be reimbursable.

cases.question: Can I just give them apple slices for snack today?
cases.facts: The meal is a snack. The snack contains one component only, fruit.
cases.correct: No. A snack with only one component is not reimbursable; it needs two of the five components.
cases.wrong: Yes, fruit on its own is a reimbursable snack.

cases.question: Can the 4 year olds have chocolate milk at lunch?
cases.facts: The meal is lunch. The child is 4 years old. The milk is flavored.
cases.correct: No. Children aged 1 through 5 must be served unflavored milk, so flavored milk is not allowed for a 4 year old.
cases.wrong: Yes, flavored milk is fine at lunch for a 4 year old.

cases.question: The school-age kids want chocolate milk at snack. Can the 7 year olds have it?
cases.facts: The meal is a snack. The child is 7 years old. The milk is flavored low-fat milk.
cases.correct: Yes. Children 6 years old and older may be served flavored milk.
cases.wrong: No. Flavored milk is not allowed for any child in the program.

cases.question: Maya just turned one. What milk does she get?
cases.facts: The child is 1 year old.
cases.correct: A child who is 1 year old must be served unflavored whole milk.
cases.wrong: A child who is 1 year old may be served low-fat milk.

cases.question: Is skim milk okay for the 3 year olds?
cases.facts: The child is 3 years old. The milk is unflavored fat-free milk.
cases.correct: Yes. Unflavored fat-free milk is creditable as fluid milk for a 3 year old; children 2 through 5 must have unflavored milk.
cases.wrong: No. Children 2 through 5 must be served whole milk only.

cases.question: We are out of milk. Can I give the 3 year olds yogurt instead of milk at lunch?
cases.facts: The meal is lunch. The child is 3 years old. Yogurt is being served in place of fluid milk.
cases.correct: No. For children, yogurt does not count as fluid milk and may not be served in place of it.
cases.wrong: Yes, 6 ounces of yogurt can replace the milk for a child once a day.

cases.question: They had orange juice at breakfast. Can apple juice be the fruit at lunch too?
cases.facts: Fruit juice was already served to meet the fruit requirement at breakfast today. The meal is lunch.
cases.correct: No. Juice may be served to meet the fruit or vegetable requirement at only one meal or snack per day, so juice at lunch does not credit.
cases.wrong: Yes, juice can be the fruit at both breakfast and lunch.

cases.question: Can pasteurized orange juice be the fruit at breakfast?
cases.facts: The meal is breakfast. The juice is pasteurized full-strength fruit juice. No juice has been served yet today.
cases.correct: Yes. Pasteurized full-strength fruit juice may be used to meet the fruit requirement at one meal or snack per day.
cases.wrong: No, juice never counts as a fruit in the program.

cases.question: Do I need a whole grain today? Breakfast was white toast and lunch is white rice.
cases.facts: No whole grain-rich grain has been served today.
cases.correct: Yes. At least one grain serving each day must be whole grain-rich, so the whole grain-rich requirement is not met yet today.
cases.wrong: No. The whole grain-rich requirement is met today.

cases.question: Breakfast was whole wheat toast. Does that cover the whole grain rule for today?
cases.facts: A whole grain-rich grain was served today at breakfast.
cases.correct: Yes. One whole grain-rich serving across the day meets the daily whole grain-rich requirement.
cases.wrong: No. Every grain served in the day must be whole grain-rich.

cases.question: Can the oatmeal cookies be the grain at snack?
cases.facts: The meal is a snack. The food is a cookie, a grain-based dessert.
cases.correct: No. Grain-based desserts such as cookies do not count toward the grains requirement.
cases.wrong: Yes, oatmeal cookies count as a grain because they are made with oats.

cases.question: Can I serve eggs instead of toast at breakfast again? That would be the fourth time this week.
cases.facts: The meal is breakfast. A meat or meat alternate has already replaced the grains component 3 times this week.
cases.correct: No. A meat or meat alternate may replace the grains at breakfast at most 3 times per week, so a fourth time does not meet the grains requirement.
cases.wrong: Yes, eggs can replace the grain at breakfast any day of the week.

cases.question: Can I serve eggs instead of toast at breakfast? It would be the second time this week.
cases.facts: The meal is breakfast. A meat or meat alternate has replaced the grains component once this week so far.
cases.correct: Yes. A meat or meat alternate may replace the entire grains component at breakfast up to 3 times per week.
cases.wrong: No. A meat or meat alternate may never replace the grain at breakfast.

cases.question: Lunch is milk, chicken, rice and pear. Is that a full lunch?
cases.facts: The meal is lunch. The meal contains fluid milk, a meat, a grain and a fruit, and no vegetable.
cases.correct: No. A reimbursable lunch must contain all five components, and this lunch has no vegetable.
cases.wrong: Yes, four components is enough for a reimbursable lunch.

cases.question: I have no fruit today. Can I serve carrots and green beans at lunch instead of a fruit?
cases.facts: The meal is lunch. A vegetable is served to meet the fruit requirement, and the two vegetables are two different kinds.
cases.correct: Yes. At lunch a vegetable may be served to meet the entire fruit requirement, provided the two vegetables are different kinds.
cases.wrong: No. A fruit must always be served at lunch and a vegetable cannot replace it.

cases.question: Can I deep fry the chicken nuggets for lunch?
cases.facts: The meal is lunch. The food is deep-fat fried on site.
cases.correct: No. Deep-fat fried foods prepared on site cannot be part of a reimbursable meal.
cases.wrong: Yes, how the chicken is cooked does not affect whether the meal is reimbursable.

cases.question: Can the 9 month old have a little apple juice at snack?
cases.facts: The participant is an infant aged 9 months. Fruit juice is served.
cases.correct: No. Fruit juice and vegetable juice must not be served to infants, and an infant meal that includes juice is not reimbursable.
cases.wrong: Yes, a small amount of juice is fine for an infant at snack.

cases.question: Does the whole grain rule apply to the 10 month old?
cases.facts: The participant is an infant aged 10 months.
cases.correct: No. The whole grain-rich requirement does not apply to infants; it applies only to the child and adult meal patterns.
cases.wrong: Yes, every participant including infants must have one whole grain-rich serving a day.

cases.question: Can I give the 11 month old some cooked rice as her grain?
cases.facts: The participant is an infant aged 11 months. The food is cooked rice.
cases.correct: No. Cooked grains such as rice, quinoa and pasta are not creditable in the infant meal pattern.
cases.wrong: Yes, cooked rice is a creditable grain for infants.

cases.question: Can cheese spread be the meat alternate for the 8 month old?
cases.facts: The participant is an infant aged 8 months. The food is cheese spread.
cases.correct: No. Cheese food and cheese spread are not creditable as a meat alternate for infants.
cases.wrong: Yes, cheese spread credits as a meat alternate for infants like any cheese.
cases.source: CACFP 06-2025, Meats and Meat Alternates, p. 13

cases.question: Does the baby cereal have to be iron fortified?
cases.facts: The participant is an infant. The infant cereal is not iron-fortified.
cases.correct: Yes. Infant cereal must be iron-fortified to be creditable.
cases.wrong: No, any infant cereal is creditable whether or not it has iron.

off_topic.question: What is the staff to child ratio for infants in Texas?
off_topic.answer: One adult for every four infants.
off_topic.why: State licensing ratios are not in 7 CFR 226.20.

off_topic.question: How much do I get paid for a lunch at tier 1?
off_topic.answer: The tier 1 lunch rate is 3.31 dollars.
off_topic.why: Reimbursement rates are published separately each July, not in the meal pattern.

off_topic.question: How much chicken does a 4 year old need at lunch?
off_topic.why: Tally's rulebook deliberately leaves portion sizes out; the tool must not claim to prove them.

off_topic.question: How long should nap time be for the 2 year olds?
off_topic.why: Not a food program question at all.
